name: Diocletian's Palace
label: Diocletian's Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Prva Vidilica' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Prva vidilica' (node/850150112): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/124205148: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Diocletian's Palace' (358 m across).
notes: Roman imperial palace that forms the heart of Split's old town.

text.description:
Diocletian's Palace is the Roman heart of Split. The emperor Diocletian built it at the end of the third century AD as his retirement home. About half was for his own use and the rest housed the garrison. Today it makes up around half of the old town, and people still live, work and eat inside its walls. It has been continuously occupied since the 7th century, when refugees from nearby Salona sheltered there. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1979.

From ground level the palace is hard to take in, because you are inside it. The best overall picture is from above which is Prva Vidilica, the first viewpoint on Marjan hill. From this terrace you look back east over the palace walls and the terracotta roofs, with the harbour and the Riva in front. It is a reasonably short walk from the old town and usually quieter than the sunset spots higher up the hill.

Keep the roofs and the line of the walls as the main subject, and let the water give the picture depth. For a different angle, walk down to the Riva, where the southern wall and the Bronze Gate sit against the harbour. The Peristil courtyard inside shows the palace from within.
text.geographic_location: Diocletian's Palace sits in the centre of Split, on the harbour front beside the Riva, and forms about half of the old town.
text.directions_text: Start in the old town near the Riva and head west on foot, then climb the stairs and paths up Marjan to the first viewpoint, Prva Vidilica. It is a roughly 15-minute walk up stairs and paths from the old town. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the whole view of walls, roofs and harbour. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), it is useful for picking out roof detail and the palace walls. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the terrace railing or foreground in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Prva Vidilica (first Marjan viewpoint, looking back east over the old town). The palace walls and terracotta roofs of the old town spread out below, with the harbour and Riva in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the palace walls and roofs on the lower third, with the harbour and sky filling the rest. Keep the phone level so the rooflines stay straight. For a different view, the Riva shows the southern wall and Bronze Gate with palm trees and boats in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the roofs to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. Try a panorama if you want the full sweep of the old town and waterfront.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise is recommended by one photography guide, for the eastern light on the city.

text.access_note: The Prva Vidilica terrace is an open public viewpoint, and the palace streets are part of the living old town, but some individual sights inside may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: A telephoto lens helps to pick out roof and wall detail from the terrace at this distance.
Keeping the phone level helps keep rooflines straight.
Dragging the exposure slider down slightly helps keep colour in the sky.

name: Bačvice
label: Bačvice Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hatzeov perivoj' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hatzeov perivoj' (way/142955072): middle (100 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM R17866195 (Bačvice): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: Bačvice is Split's busy town beach, a sandy bay with the open Adriatic in front and the city behind. It photographs well because there is always something going on: swimmers, games in the shallows and people strolling along the edge of the bay. The best phone view is not from the sand itself. Hatzeov perivoj is the beach park on the road above, and its shaded benches look down over the beach, the bay and the activity below. That height lets you fit the curve of the shoreline and the water into one frame without crowds in the foreground. It is also a quieter elevated alternative to the crowded sand. If you want a different angle, the sandy bay itself shows the crescent of the beach with the Split waterfront and city behind. The rocky western end is called Pomoraca Park, and from there you get a lower view along the coast. That end involves some climbing and is not a formal lookout, so take care there. Be aware that building work around the bay can sometimes get into the view, so check your frame before you take the shot. Wipe your lens before you start, because sea air and sunscreen smear it quickly.
text.geographic_location: Bačvice is the sandy bay beach on Split's coast, with the beach park of Hatzeov perivoj on the road above the sand.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Split and make your way to the Bačvice bay. Hatzeov perivoj is the beach's own address, so it is a useful name to look for. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole curve of the bay, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out swimmers or the far shoreline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Hatzeov perivoj (the beach park on the road above the sand). A looking-down view over the beach, the bay and the activity on the sand from the shaded park above. From the high ground, and from the shaded benches of the park nearby, you look down over the beach, the bay and the activity on the sand, with the beach itself lying to the south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the waterline along the lower third, so the bay and sky fill the rest. Keep a tree branch or the park edge at one side for depth. If you want a different view, the sandy bay itself shows the crescent of the beach with the city behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the water or the sand to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sea and sand do not wash out. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of the waves and swimmers.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier or later in the day usually gives softer light than at midday.

text.access_note: Hatzeov perivoj is an open public park and Bačvice is a public beach, but check the official site before you go if you want to know about any building work around the bay.

name: Marjan
label: Marjan Hill
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Riva' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Riva' (relation/1679868): middle (335 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9342886: large area 'Marjan Forest Park' (3893 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Forested hill with viewpoints over the old town and the islands.

text.description:
Marjan is the green hill at the western end of Split's peninsula. It is covered in dense Mediterranean pine forest and surrounded by the city and the sea, which is why it stands out so clearly from town. It is about 178 m high, and it is a favourite weekend excursion and recreation area for Split people, with walks, jogging trails and beaches. Its use as a park goes back a very long way: Diocletian's palace stood a short walk away, and the emperor laid out the nearer slopes as a park. Over the last century and a half the hill has become a symbol of Split.

The easiest way to photograph Marjan itself is from the city, not from the hill. From the western end of the Riva promenade you can see the wooded slopes rising behind the seafront, with the waterfront in the foreground. That gives the picture a sense of place: dark green hill, pale buildings, open water. Keep the hill as the main subject and use a bit of promenade or sea to anchor the frame. If you have the time, the old harbour-side Venecijanska kula makes a good foreground with the pine slopes behind it. Kašjuni Beach shows the quieter, cliffier southern side of the hill.

The Riva is a busy, open promenade, so take a few frames and step aside to check them rather than stopping in the walkway.
text.geographic_location: Marjan is the wooded hill at the western end of Split's peninsula, west of the old centre and Diocletian's Palace. The suggested photo spot is at the western end of the Riva, the seafront promenade.
text.directions_text: Head for the Riva, the seafront promenade in the centre of Split, and walk to its western end. No public transport stops near this spot were identified in the data; the Riva can be reached on foot from the centre of Split. Once there, look west and Marjan is the large wooded hill ahead of you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole waterfront with the hill behind. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the hill closer and fill the frame with the pine slopes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Riva (western end, looking west toward the hill). Marjan's wooded slopes rising behind the seafront and the city's waterfront, photographed from the promenade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the hill's ridge line on the upper third, with the promenade or water along the bottom third. Keep the horizon level. For a different view, Venecijanska kula makes a strong foreground with the pine slopes behind it, and Kašjuni Beach gives a quieter shot of the hill's southern side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hill to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the pines stay dark green. If people pass in front of you, hold the shutter or use Live Photos/motion and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning to early afternoon is usually the safest choice, when the sun is behind or beside you and lights the hill rather than shining into your lens. Late in the day the sun sets behind the hill, so expect a darker, backlit shot.

text.access_note: The Riva is a public promenade and Marjan is a public forest park. Access to the Venecijanska kula was not checked.
claims_not_in_sources: The Riva is a busy promenade where people walk through the frame.
Looking west from the Riva, the sun sets behind Marjan, so late-day shots are backlit.
In the morning and early afternoon the sun is behind or beside someone looking west, so the hill is front-lit.
Venecijanska kula and Kašjuni Beach are suggested as alternative viewpoints, and the tower's access was not checked.

name: Riva
label: Riva Promenade
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Trg Republike' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Trg Republike' (way/142921077): middle (120 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM R1679868 (Riva): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Palm-lined waterfront promenade in front of the palace's south wall.

text.description: The Riva is Split's long, pedestrian waterfront promenade. It photographs well because several things line up in one frame: a row of palm trees, the honey-coloured wall of Diocletian's Palace behind them, and the harbour and boats beside you. For a calmer, more composed picture, start at Trg Republike, the square at the west end of the Riva where the promenade meets the square. Guides compare it with St Mark's Square in Venice and praise its symmetry. Buildings frame the space on both sides, and you also get a glimpse of the harbour and the Riva. Put yourself in the middle, switch on the gridlines and keep the buildings level on both sides, and the photo almost composes itself. Then walk the 200 m or so along the promenade and shoot back along the palms and the palace wall from near the water's edge. If you are here near sunset, the small fishermen's harbour at Matejuška is a good alternative. Boats and strolling silhouettes are lit from behind by the setting sun. The Riva is a pedestrian promenade with no closures known, so you can try several angles. Keep your phone lens clean, as sea air and fingers smudge it quickly.
text.geographic_location: On Split's harbour front, along the promenade that runs beside the old town and Diocletian's Palace.
text.directions_text: Head for Split's old-town waterfront on foot or by local transport, and go to Trg Republike at the west end of the Riva. Walk along the promenade with the harbour on your side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) at the square to fit in the buildings on both sides. Along the promenade, use the default lens (1x) for the palms and palace wall. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for picking out boats and strollers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Trg Republike (west end of the Riva, where the promenade meets the square). A symmetrical view of the square, with buildings framing the space and a glimpse of the harbour and Riva. The Riva itself is to the south-east, so walk that way for the palm-and-palace-wall shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: At the square, stand on the centre line and use the gridlines to keep both sides balanced and the verticals straight. On the Riva, go to the water's edge so the row of palms leads the eye towards the palace wall. For a different take, Matejuška's fishermen's harbour gives boats and silhouettes against the sun.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building facades to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky keeps its colour. For the Matejuška silhouettes, tap on the sky and drag the exposure down. Try a Live Photo to catch people walking through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: For the Matejuška silhouettes, go near sunset. Earlier or later in the day is usually kinder to the square and the palace wall than harsh midday light.

text.access_note: The Riva is an open public promenade and Trg Republike is an open square, with no closures known, but check the official site before you go if you plan anything beyond walking and photographing.

name: Poljud Stadium
label: Poljud Stadium
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ulica Stjepana Radića' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Ulica Stjepana Radića nearest the subject (our map tiles); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/142675682: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Poljud Stadium' (314 m across).
notes: Seaside home ground of Hajduk Split with a shell-like roof.

text.description:
Poljud Stadium is the home ground of Hajduk Split, and it looks unlike most football grounds. Architect Boris Magaš designed it as a great concrete shell, and the roof spans 206 by 47 metres. It opened in September 1979 and now seats 33,987 people, down from an original capacity of 55,000. In 2015 it was officially recognised as cultural heritage.

The roof is the reason to bring your phone. Its long curved edge makes a bold shape that is easy to read in a single frame, so you don't need to be clever with the composition. The stadium sits slightly below the level of the surrounding roads, and the landscaped area around it is meant for walking. That gives you room to step back and take in the whole building.

A separate recommended viewpoint for the full roof profile is Ulica Stjepana Radića, at the junction with the northern approach road. It lies to the north of the stadium, so you face south from there. Nothing gets in the way at that junction. A second option is the south approach, where the roof and concrete structure appear with the sea and nearby houses behind.

Keep the whole roof in the frame and let the sky fill the top third. Check the edges of the picture for lamp posts and parked cars before you press the shutter. Reconstruction work was expected to start in 2025, so you may see scaffolding or closed sections. Drone photography is generally prohibited here, so keep to your phone.
text.geographic_location: Poljud Stadium is in the Poljud neighbourhood, part of Split's Spinut district.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot. From there the stadium is 109 m to the north-west. If you also want the northern viewpoint, it is a separate spot: the junction of Ulica Stjepana Radića and the northern approach road, north of the stadium, where you face south. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole roof from where you stand. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the roof will not fit. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the concrete and the roof edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ulica Stjepana Radića (junction with the northern approach road, facing south toward the stadium). The full curved roof of the stadium in a single frame, seen from the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the roof edge up with a horizontal grid line so the curve looks balanced. Keep the whole roof in the frame, with some sky above it and a little foreground below. For a different view, try the south approach, where the shell-shaped roof appears with the sea and houses behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the roof to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little. This stops the bright sky from washing out the concrete. If the roof will not fit, try panorama mode, and hold the phone level as you sweep.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light in the morning or late afternoon usually flatters concrete and avoids harsh shadows under the roof. On match days the area around the stadium is likely to be busier.

text.access_note: Access around the stadium can change on match days and during the building work, so check the official site before you go. Pitch-side views are only available on a stadium tour.

name: Cathedral of Saint Domnius
label: Cathedral & Bell Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Peristil' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Peristil' (way/29704912): middle (48 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/272588434: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cathedral of Saint Domnius' (52 m across).
notes: Former mausoleum of Diocletian with a tower that gives views over the old town.

text.description:
The Cathedral of Saint Domnius began life in AD 305 as the mausoleum of the Roman emperor Diocletian, and it is still used as a cathedral today. Its eight-sided outline, once ringed by a covered walkway of 24 columns, sits inside Diocletian's Palace, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The bell tower beside it rises to 57 metres and is easy to spot, so it is easy to find and easy to frame.

The classic photo is taken from the Peristil, the sunken Roman courtyard in the palace. From there the bell tower and facade rise above the columns, with the Protiron arch and the palace colonnade around them. Guides treat this as the standard view of the cathedral and the most photographed spot in the palace.

The cathedral is also known for its walnut doors, carved in 1214 by Andrija Buvina. They have 28 scenes from the life of Christ, and very few medieval wooden doors survive in such good condition. Photography inside is generally permitted, but be discreet and never use flash during services.

If you want a second view, the Riva waterfront has palm trees and old buildings in front, with the bell tower rising behind over the harbour. Treat that as a quick alternative and see how it looks on the day.
text.geographic_location: The bell tower rises directly above it.
text.directions_text: Head for the old town and Diocletian's Palace, then continue on foot to the Peristil courtyard. Once you are inside the palace walls, look up for the bell tower; it shows you which way to go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the colonnade, the arch and the tall bell tower into one frame. Then try the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. A telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for the top of the bell tower and the carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Peristil (stand at the southern end near the Protiron arch and look north up the colonnade). The cathedral's bell tower and facade rise above the columned courtyard, framed by the Protiron arch and the palace columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the bell tower on one of the vertical lines, with the columns framing each side. Hold the phone level, because tilting it upwards makes the tower lean. If people are in the way, wait a moment and take several shots, or use them to show the size of the courtyard. For a different view, try the Riva waterfront, with the palm trees in the foreground and the tower behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright stone of the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and pale stone don't wash out. Live Photos can catch people moving through the courtyard, but keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, around 6:30 to 8:00 in summer, when the square is least crowded.

text.access_note: The Peristil viewpoint is free. The cathedral is a working place of worship, so dress modestly and be quiet. Entry arrangements and the bell tower climb may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: A narrow courtyard makes the ultra-wide lens helpful for fitting in a tall bell tower.
Tilting the phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean.
Dressing modestly is expected when visiting an active cathedral.

photo.artist: Original uploader was Karlo Šiljeg at hr.wikipedia

name: Froggyland
label: Froggyland
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/6612952014: the OpenStreetMap point 'Froggyland'.
notes: Museum of stuffed frogs posed in everyday scenes.

text.description:
Froggyland is a small museum in Split with an unusual collection: 21 little scenes in which 507 stuffed frogs are posed as if they were doing everyday human things, such as playing poker, sitting in a classroom or performing in a circus. It photographs well because the idea is so odd and the scenes are so detailed. Each diorama is a tiny story, and a phone can capture one in a single frame.

The frogs were prepared by Ferenc Mere, who was born in 1878 and worked on them between 1910 and 1920, using the edible frog. He started with over 1000 frogs, but only 507 survive. The collection was found in an attic in Serbia, and in 1970 the parents of the current owner bought it and brought it to Split. The museum has also drawn criticism from people who see the use of the frogs as cruel, so you may want to be sensitive about how you share your pictures.

For photos, pick one scene at a time and fill the frame with it, rather than trying to capture a whole room. Look for the funniest expression or the most elaborate prop, and keep the background simple. If you want a shot of the museum from outside, the phone icon on the map is right at its location. Rules on photography inside, and on using flash, may apply, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Froggyland is in the city of Split, Croatia.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head to the museum's location on the map by whatever local route suits you. Once you arrive, you are already at the phone icon on the map. Check the official site for the exact entrance before you set off. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if a room feels too tight to fit a whole diorama in. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), it is good for picking out one frog's face without leaning in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you can photograph the building and its entrance, and the scenes inside if photography is allowed.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up each diorama so the scene sits level and fills most of the frame. Choose one clear story, such as the card game or the classroom, and keep your own reflection out of the shot by standing slightly off-centre.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the nearest frog to focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down a little so the scene is not washed out. Portrait mode can help a single frog stand out from its background, if the phone copes with the small subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a quieter moment if you can, so you have time to frame each scene without people in the way. Check the official site for visiting times.

text.access_note: Froggyland is a museum, so entry and photography rules may apply; check the official site before you go.

name: Ivan Meštrović Gallery
label: Meštrović Gallery
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/84629308: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Galerija Meštrović' (56 m across).
notes: Sculptor's former villa with his works, near Marjan.

text.description:
The Ivan Meštrović Gallery is an art museum in a stone villa on the Marjan peninsula, west of Split's old centre. It is dedicated to the 20th-century sculptor Ivan Meštrović, who designed the house himself as a family home, a working studio and a place to show his work. It was built between 1931 and 1939 and looks over the Adriatic. The gallery was founded after he donated the property to the state in 1952, and a renovated permanent display opened on 18 May 1998.

It photographs well because the building and its sculptures work together. The formal stone façade gives you clean lines and strong shapes, and eight bronze sculptures stand in the park in front of the building, so you can put a figure in the foreground with the villa behind it. The building itself is also described as an artistic monument, so it is worth photographing as a subject in its own right and not just as a backdrop.

For a phone, keep it simple. Start with a wide view of the whole façade, then move closer for a sculpture with a slice of the villa behind it. Switch on the gridlines so the vertical lines of the building stay straight. If a statue is in bright sun and the stone is pale, tap on the stone and pull the exposure slider down a little so the detail does not wash out. Inside, photography rules may differ, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: On the Marjan peninsula, on the western side of Split, in a park-like garden overlooking the Adriatic Sea. It is not far from the Kaštelet-Crikvine chapel.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stop is listed for this spot, so start from Split's old centre and head west towards the Marjan peninsula, then use a map app to find the gallery. The phone icon on the map shows exactly where to take the photo. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole façade and the sculptures in front of it, then use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of a sculpture or the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. To frame the whole façade, step back within the grounds or the park until the villa fits comfortably in the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the façade with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Use one of the bronze sculptures in the park as a foreground subject, with the villa behind it. Take one wide shot of the whole building, then move closer for a tighter shot of one figure against the stone wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone façade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the pale stone looks too bright. Use portrait mode on a sculpture only if the edges look clean; otherwise stay with the normal photo mode.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the light is soft and the façade is not in harsh glare, such as the morning or later in the afternoon. Check which side of the building is lit when you arrive.

text.access_note: This is a museum with a sculpture park, so access may be ticketed and hours may change: check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The villa's façade is pale stone that can look bright in strong sun.
Softer light in the morning or later afternoon is usually more flattering for pale stone.
Phone photography inside the museum may be restricted, so rules should be checked.

name: Temple of Jupiter
label: Temple of Jupiter
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Peristil' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Peristil' (way/29704912): middle (48 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/124199046: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Temple of Jupiter' (21 m across).
notes: Roman temple, later a baptistery, with a sphinx at its entrance.

text.description:
The Temple of Jupiter is a small Roman temple tucked into the western part of Diocletian's Palace, close to the Peristil, the palace's central square. It was built between 295 and 305 as part of the palace and dedicated to Jupiter. It was later turned into a baptistery, probably in the 6th century. It photographs well because so much is packed into a small space: carved reliefs of gods and heroes above the doorway, a Romanesque bell tower added in the 11th century, and a sphinx brought from Egypt standing in front of the entrance. The Scottish architect Robert Adam thought it one of the most beautiful monuments in Europe.

From there you get the wider context shot: the square with the Protyron arch framing the view. The temple itself is a short walk to the west, so walk over for the close-up of the entrance. There, include the sphinx in the foreground and the reliefs above the door. The lanes are narrow and the square can be busy, so be patient and take your time over each shot. Inside, the vaulted ceiling is the main sight, but it needs a paid combined palace ticket, so check the official site before you go. Photography is generally allowed inside, but look for signs on the day.
text.geographic_location: In the western part of Diocletian's Palace, in Split's old town, just west of the Peristil (the palace's central square).
text.directions_text: Head for Diocletian's Palace in the old town and finish on foot. Walk to the Peristil, the palace's central square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the temple's entrance with the sphinx. Switch to 2x or 3x (the longest zoom your phone has, up to 5x) from the steps of the Peristil to pick out the arch and details in a busy square. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you can step back, as it stretches the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Peristil (the steps at the edge of the square, with the Protyron arch as a frame). The palace's central square with the Protyron arch framing the view, a short walk east of the temple, useful as a wider context shot. For the temple itself, walk west to its entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines. On the Peristil, put the Protyron arch in the middle of the frame and let the steps lead the eye towards it. At the temple, keep the sphinx low in the foreground and the carved reliefs above the doorway at the top, holding the phone upright to fit it all in. The Jupiterov hram entrance is the best alternative view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the temple's stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the pale stone keeps its detail. Take a Live Photo if people are crossing the square. You can pick the cleanest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before 9am, when the Peristil is nearly empty and the light is better.

text.access_note: The outside and the square are open to walk around, but the temple interior needs a paid combined palace ticket, so check the official site before you go.

name: Statue of Gregory of Nin
label: Gregory of Nin
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Peristil' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Peristil' (way/29704912): middle (48 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM N4221604987 (Gregory of Nin): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Meštrović bronze whose toe is rubbed for luck.

text.description:
The bronze statue of Gregory of Nin, the bishop shown with one arm raised, stands just outside the Golden Gate of Diocletian's Palace, on Kralja Tomislava. It is about 7.6 to 8.5 metres tall, and accounts differ on the exact height. It was moved to this spot from the Peristyle in 1954. The Golden Gate stands right beside it, so you can photograph the statue and the old stonework together.

It photographs well because of its size and its setting. Stand back and the whole figure fits in one frame with the gate behind it. Come closer and look up, and the raised arm and upper body stand out against the sky. A full-length view with the Golden Gate behind is the classic shot. A tighter shot of the upper body is a good second one.

One guide suggests the steps for a view with palace columns, but the statue is not there now, so check on the ground. Use the steps for a shot of the setting if the view works, and walk north to the statue for the main picture. The statue is in the open and is free to visit at any hour. Midday brings crowds from cruise ships, so go early if you want a clear frame.
text.geographic_location: In the old town of Split, on Kralja Tomislava just outside the Golden Gate of Diocletian's Palace. The Peristyle, the palace's central square, is a short walk to the south.
text.directions_text: Start from the Peristyle in the middle of the old town and walk north to the Golden Gate. It is on Kralja Tomislava, beside the Golden Gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the statue with the Golden Gate behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough to fit the whole figure. Use telephoto (2x-3x, or up to 5x if your phone has it) for the upper body and raised arm against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Peristil (from the Peristyle steps). A quieter, framed view that includes palace columns, offered as a way to give the statue a sense of scale. One guide suggests the steps for a view with palace columns, but the statue is not there now, so check on the ground. Check the view on the spot, then walk north for the close-up shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: At the statue, step back until the whole bronze figure and the Golden Gate fit in one frame, and turn on gridlines to keep the walls straight. For a second shot, move closer, hold the phone low and use the zoom to catch the raised arm against the sky. Another place to try is the open space near the gate, for the full figure with the gate behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bronze keeps its detail and the sky does not turn white. Avoid portrait mode, as it can blur the edges of the figure.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the tour groups reach the Peristyle and the gate. Midday is usually the busiest time, with cruise-ship visitors.

text.access_note: The statue is in an open public space beside the Golden Gate and is free to see at any hour; check the official site before you go if you plan to enter the palace itself.
claims_not_in_sources: The Peristyle lies south of the Golden Gate, so the statue may not be clearly visible from the Peristyle steps.
A low camera angle and zoom can isolate the raised arm against the sky.
Bronze against a bright sky can lose detail unless the exposure is lowered slightly.

name: Cellars of Diocletian's Palace
label: Palace Cellars
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/8857605118: the OpenStreetMap point 'Basement Halls of Diocletian's Palace'.
notes: Vaulted Roman basement halls, among the best-preserved parts of the palace.

text.description: The cellars lie under the southern end of Diocletian's Palace, in the southernmost part of Split's Old Town. They once held up the Emperor's private apartments, and they are among the best preserved ancient structures of their kind anywhere. Their layout closely follows the rooms that were above, so walking through them gives a good idea of the palace's original plan. The cellars cover roughly an eighth of the palace's area. In Roman times they were also used to store food and wine, and the remains of a large press can still be seen. They photograph well because of the massive barrel vaults, the plain stone walls and the way the rooms open into one another. In the Middle Ages some of the space was lived in, and later it filled with rubbish. Excavation began in the 19th century. The western halls opened to visitors in 1959 and the eastern part in 1996. Interior light may be low, so work with what you have. Look for repeating arches that lead the eye down a hall, and for the wine press as a close-up subject with the vault behind it. Keep your elbows in, move slowly and give other visitors room. Check the official site before you go for current access and any photography rules.
text.geographic_location: In the southern part of Diocletian's Palace, which forms the southernmost part of Split's Old Town, below the Emperor's former private apartments.
text.directions_text: Head for Split's Old Town and Diocletian's Palace. The cellars are at the southern end of the palace. You can enter through the Bronze Gate or down a staircase from the Peristyle. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the length of a vaulted hall into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the wine press and other details. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) only for far-off arches, and expect more grain if the light is low.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face along the hall to get the arches receding in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the centre of the vault with the middle vertical line, so the arches look even on both sides. Keep the phone level, because tilted walls are very noticeable in a symmetrical space. Take one wide shot of the hall, then move closer for a detail such as the wine press or a stone doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-tone part of the wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so any bright doorway or lit area is not washed out. Let night mode work if it switches on, and hold the phone against your body or a wall for the second or two it needs.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a quiet moment, as fewer people in the frame makes the vaults look much better and gives cleaner frames. Check the official site before you go for current visiting times.

text.access_note: Access and any ticket or photography rules may apply, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Interior light may be low, so phone photos may need night mode or a brighter exposure.
Quieter times, such as early or late in the day, are likely to give cleaner frames with fewer people.
The Bronze Gate is at the southern edge of the palace.
Entry is likely to need a ticket, and photography rules may apply, so visitors should check the official site.

name: Golden Gate
label: Golden Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Zlatna vrata' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/327191536: the OpenStreetMap point 'Golden Gate'.
notes: Northern gate of the palace with the Gregory of Nin statue nearby.

text.description: The Golden Gate is the northern entrance to Diocletian's Palace, set in the middle of the old town's north wall. It is one of four main Roman gates into the palace, and it was built to look grand. The stonework is the reason to photograph it. Above the opening is an arch made of 19 stone blocks, and the front has five niches and a row of small blind arches. Look closely at the little carved faces under the brackets above the doorway. The gate was sealed off in the Middle Ages and lost its columns and statues. It was only reopened in 1857, and it was wrapped for restoration from 2012 until 2015. The gate was also once flanked by two octagonal towers, which are now gone. The classic frame is from outside, on the north face. Meštrović's bronze statue of Bishop Gregory of Nin stands in front of the gate, so you can get the statue and the old stone in one picture. A second option is the inner side of the gate, looking back through the arch to the street and the statue beyond. Expect crowds around midday, when cruise and tour groups come through. If you want fewer people in the shot, go early, shortly after sunrise, or in the evening when the stone looks warmer. Costumed Roman soldiers sometimes pose for photos here.
text.geographic_location: The Golden Gate is in the middle of the northern wall of Diocletian's Palace, on the edge of Split's old town (stari grad). It is the gate that faces north.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so start from Split old town and head for the middle of the palace's northern wall, where the gate stands. Inside the palace, the inner side of the gate opens onto the Cardo Maximus, the long straight street that runs the other way to the Bronze Gate. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the gate, the statue and the walls in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the niches, the arch and the small carved faces above the doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the gate's arch and flanking walls frame the bronze statue of Bishop Gregory of Nin in front. For a second frame, go through to the inner side and shoot back through the arch, with the street and statue visible beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the arch centred, with the statue slightly to one side so it does not hide the doorway. Hold the phone level so the stone courses stay straight. Then step closer or zoom in for the carved details. The inner side of the gate makes a good alternative frame, with the arch acting as a natural border.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the gate does not turn into a silhouette. If people keep walking through the frame, try a Live Photo or take a quick burst and choose the clearest one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, shortly after sunrise, or in the evening when the stone warms in low light, according to one guide. Midday is the busiest time.

text.access_note: The gate is an open public space that is free to see and open all day, but check the official site before you go in case that changes.

name: Peristyle of Diocletian's Palace
label: Peristyle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Vestibul' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Vestibul' (relation/9493968): middle (28 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/124205148: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Diocletian's Palace' (358 m across).
notes: The central colonnaded courtyard of the palace.

text.description:
The Peristyle is the colonnaded open courtyard at the heart of Diocletian's Palace, the Roman retirement residence that Emperor Diocletian had built at the end of the third century AD. Today the palace makes up about half of Split's old town and around 3,000 people live inside it, so the old columns stand in a working town rather than a roped-off ruin. UNESCO listed the palace as a World Heritage Site in 1979.

It photographs well because of the rhythm of the columns, the pale stone paving and the cathedral bell tower at the far end. The cathedral sits in the building first put up as a temple and later used as Diocletian's Mausoleum. Its Romanesque bell tower was completed in the medieval period, between the 12th and 14th centuries.

For something a little different from the crowded middle of the courtyard, try the Vestibul, the domed entrance hall just south of the Peristyle. Stand inside the archway and look back out: the arch becomes a natural frame around the columns. One guide calls this one of the most photogenic angles in Split, and it is a quieter spot than the central courtyard. Take a few frames from the courtyard too, to show the full length of the colonnade. The polished stone is very slippery when wet, so watch your step while you are looking at your screen. Street performers may ask for payment if you photograph them.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Split's old town, inside the walls of Diocletian's Palace, with the cathedral and its bell tower at the far end of the courtyard.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, so it is reached on foot through the old town and in through the palace walls. It is about 1 minute on foot between the two. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) inside the Vestibul to take in the domed hall and the whole arch. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier frame around the columns. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull in the colonnade and bell tower from the archway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Vestibul (inside the archway looking back out toward the Peristyle). A framed view through the Vestibule's archway out onto the colonnaded Peristyle. The Peristyle opens out in front of you, framed by the arch, with the colonnade ahead.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the arch up with the frame edges so the columns stay upright. Let the dark stone of the arch form a border around the bright courtyard. If you want the whole colonnade running north with the bell tower at the end, walk out to the middle of the Peristyle and shoot from there as an alternative. Hold the phone against the archway wall to keep it steady, and don't assume you can set up a tripod in the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright courtyard to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and pale stone keep their detail. If a Live Photo is on, hold still for a moment after pressing the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit when it is least crowded to get the archway view without people in front of you.

text.access_note: The Peristyle itself is free and open to the public; the cathedral and bell tower need a ticket, so check the official site before you go.

name: Salona
label: Salona Ruins
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Amfiteatar' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Amfiteatar' (way/45421180): middle (152 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/45421178: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Starine' (332 m across).
notes: Ruins of the Roman provincial capital just north-east of Split.

text.description:
Salona was one of the largest cities of the late Roman Empire and the capital of the Roman province of Dalmatia. Today its ruins make up the largest archaeological park in Croatia. Most of the city was destroyed in the seventh century, but walls, a forum, a theatre, public baths and an aqueduct still survive. The amphitheatre is the most conspicuous of the remains above ground, and it is the best place to start with a phone.

The oval arena photographs well because its stone tiers stand in open ground, with the Solin landscape and distant hills behind. Nothing crowds the frame, so you can take wide, simple pictures that show the scale of the place. Guides often call it the most atmospheric part of the site.

For a clean angle, go to the south side and look along the outer walls, either west or east. If you have time, the early Christian church ruins at Manastirine are a quieter second stop. There the stones and sarcophagi sit among greenery, which makes for a more intimate set of pictures.

The ground is open and uneven, so watch your step while you are looking at the screen. Some gardens around the site are private, so keep to the visitor paths. Go early if you can: the light is kinder and the tour groups have not yet arrived.
text.geographic_location: Salona lies in the town of Solin, about 6 km from the centre of Split, where the ruins spread across open ground.
text.directions_text: No stations or tram stops are listed for the site, and Solin is about 6 km from the centre of Split. Ask for the amphitheatre, which is next to Entrance 2. The Main Entrance has a free car park, and you can walk to the amphitheatre from there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole oval arena and its surroundings into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the long lines of the outer walls. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the stone tiers and arches without walking onto uneven ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (south side, looking west or east along the outer walls). The oval Roman arena ruins with their stone tiers, framed by the open Solin landscape and distant hills.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the curve of the walls along a lower third line, with the hills and sky above. Keep the phone level so the stones do not lean. If the whole oval will not fit, try panorama mode, moving slowly and steadily. For a quieter alternative, Manastirine has early Christian church ruins and sarcophagi among greenery.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the sky keeps its colour and the stone keeps its texture. Take a few frames with different zoom levels, as the walls look very different at 0.5x and at 2x or more.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning, before the tour groups arrive, when the light is good and the crowds are thin.

text.access_note: The site is open ground with uneven terrain, and entry may be ticketed or have rules for equipment, so check the official site before you go.

name: Croatian National Theatre, Split
label: National Theatre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Trg Gaje Bulata' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Trg Gaje Bulata' (way/943201298): middle (133 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/12754522397: the OpenStreetMap point 'National Theater in Split'.

text.description: The Croatian National Theatre is the bright yellow building that fills one side of Trg Gaje Bulata, and the colour is the reason it works so well in a phone photo. Seen head-on from across the open square, the facade stands out clearly against the modern and older buildings around it. The theatre opened in 1893 as the Split Municipal Theatre, in the time of mayor Gajo Bulat, and was designed by local architects Emilio Vecchietti and Ante Bezić. It held about 1,000 people when Split had only 16,000 residents, and at the time it was the biggest theatre in Southeast Europe. A fire in February 1970 nearly destroyed the building, and the rebuilt theatre reopened in May 1980. It is still a working theatre today, and it is one of the oldest in Dalmatia. For the classic shot, stand in the square and face the front of the building, so the facade fills the middle of the frame with open space around it. If you would like a quieter angle, Cankareva poljana is a short walk away and gives another view of the front, but check it on the spot. The facade can look different by day and by night, so look at the light when you arrive.
text.geographic_location: In central Split, on the open square Trg Gaje Bulata, with the theatre's yellow front facing the square.
text.directions_text: Head for Trg Gaje Bulata in the centre of Split; by taxi or hired scooter, ask for the Croatian National Theatre. Once the theatre is to the west, about 1 minute on foot. No station or tram stop is given for this spot, so use the yellow facade as your landmark. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the whole facade with the square in front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the building will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the upper facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Trg Gaje Bulata (across the square, facing the front facade). The bright yellow front of the theatre framed by the open square, with the surrounding modern and old buildings in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the theatre's centre on the middle line so the facade looks straight. Keep a band of open square in the foreground to give a sense of distance. Hold the phone level to stop the sides leaning inwards. If you want a different angle, Cankareva poljana offers a quieter view of the front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the yellow wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the yellow stays rich and does not wash out. Keep portrait mode and Live Photos off for the building itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening, when the square is less shaded. Check the light when you arrive, as the facade can look different by day and at night.

text.access_note: The square is open public space, but check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside, and note that photography inside is not allowed during performances.

name: Sustipan
label: Sustipan Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sustipan' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/82164642: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sustipan' (325 m across).
notes: Small peninsula park with sea views toward the old town.

text.description:
Sustipan is a small, green peninsula on the southwestern side of Split, about 325 metres across, and it is now a forest park for strolling. The name means Saint Stephen. In the Middle Ages a Benedictine monastery and a church stood here, and in the 19th century a well-known cemetery was laid out on the peninsula. It was removed in the 20th century, so today you will find pines, paths and sea views rather than monuments.

It photographs well because of the simple mix of dark pine trunks, pale cliff edge and open water, with islands on the horizon. The best frame is at the westernmost edge of the park, on the cliff, a walk west from the map point. From there you can look back along the cliff line, with pines and sea in the foreground. It is a quieter alternative to the small neoclassical gloriette in the middle of the park, which is also worth a photo, with the pines, sea and islands behind it.

Take your time and walk the paths before choosing a frame. The cliffs drop steeply, so keep well back from the edge when you compose your shot, and never step closer for a better angle. The park is described as gated and open during the day only, so check current opening hours before you go.
text.geographic_location: Sustipan is a small peninsula in the southwestern part of Split, reaching out into the sea. It is a wooded park area at the edge of the city.
text.directions_text: Head for the southwestern part of Split, where the Sustipan peninsula juts into the sea. The map point is in the middle of the park. From there, walk west across the park to the cliff edge at its far tip for the quieter view, keeping well back from the drop. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the cliff edge, pines and sea. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the tree line and sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the gloriette or the distant islands.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the quieter view, walk to the westernmost edge, on the cliff. From there you look back along the park's cliff edge, with the pines and the sea in the foreground. Keep well back from the drop.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the cliff edge along a lower third line, with the pines on one side and the sea filling the rest. Keep your phone level so the horizon stays straight. For a different view, take a second photo of the small neoclassical gloriette in the middle of the park, with the pines, sea and islands behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pines or the cliff to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and sea keep their colour. Try panorama mode along the cliff line, moving slowly, or take a Live Photo to catch the movement of the branches.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening is a good choice, when the light is softer and the sea looks warmer. Always allow time to leave before the park closes.

text.access_note: This is a public forest park, but it is described as gated and open during the day only, so check current opening hours before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The western tip of the park faces the open sea, so late afternoon and evening light is likely to suit it.
Light in the late afternoon or early evening is softer than at midday.
Pine trees can create strong shade and contrast around midday.

name: Silver Gate
label: Silver Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Poljana kraljice Jelene' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Poljana kraljice Jelene' (way/29705045): middle (70 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/327191542: the OpenStreetMap point 'Silver Gate'.
notes: East gate of the palace, leading to the green market.

text.description:
The Silver Gate is the eastern entrance to Diocletian's Palace, the Roman complex at the heart of Split's old town. It is one of the palace's four principal gates and faces east, towards the Roman town of Epetia, now Stobreč. It was a secondary gate, less ornate than the Golden Gate on the north side, but it still has two niches that probably once held statues. It sits between two octagonal towers, with four more towers beside them that guarded this side of the palace.

It photographs well because the old stonework stands right at the edge of an open square, so you can step back and get the whole arch in one frame. The gate also has a layered history. A small church to St Apolinar was probably built above it around the 6th century, and the gate was heavily renovated in 1952. Pope John Paul II drove through it in his popemobile on the way to the cathedral during his 2000 visit.

Stand outside, in the square facing the east wall, and take your first shot of the full arch. Then look for details: the niches, the tower stonework and the upper arcade. If you step through the gate, the inner arch and upper arcade make a good second picture with the Roman stonework around them. The gate faces the Green Market, which is busy in the morning, so traffic and market stalls may get into your frame. Wait a moment for a gap, or choose a time when the square is calmer.
text.geographic_location: On the eastern side of Split's old town, in the middle of the palace's east wall, on Hrvojeva street. It faces the Green Market (Pazar) and the square in front of it, Poljana kraljice Jelene.
text.directions_text: Head for the Green Market (Pazar) on the east side of Split's old town; the Silver Gate is in the palace wall facing it. If you are coming from further away, head for the Green Market (Pazar) on the east side of the old town. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole arch. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is crowded and you cannot step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the niches and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Poljana kraljice Jelene (outside the gate, facing the east wall). The full arched east gateway of the palace, framed by the open square in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the arch up in the centre, keeping the vertical edges of the towers straight. Hold the phone level so the walls do not lean. If you want a second angle, go through the gate and photograph its inner arch and the upper arcade from the other side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky does not wash out and the stone keeps its colour. Take a few frames in case people or vehicles walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early evening, when the sun is low and lights the stonework. Mornings are busier because of the market.

text.access_note: The gate and the square outside are an open public space; check the official site before you go for anything inside the church above the gate or the neighbouring museum.
claims_not_in_sources: Hrvojeva street and the Green Market being busy in the morning comes from the viewpoint notes, not from the written sources.

name: Iron Gate
label: Iron Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Narodni trg' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Narodni trg' (way/142921052): middle (91 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1345939661: the OpenStreetMap point 'Iron Gate'.
notes: West gate next to the Church of Our Lady of the Belfry and People's Square.

text.description: The Iron Gate is the western entrance to the old town of Split, which grew out of Diocletian's Palace. It is one of the four main Roman gates and the only one that has stayed in everyday use right up to today. What you see is a stone archway with a clock set into the front and a medieval bell tower beside it. The gate no longer holds its iron door, only the arch and the slot for the mechanism. It photographs well because of the layers of history in one small frame: Roman stonework, a later clock and a pre-Romanesque tower. The bell tower dates from the 11th century and is described as the oldest preserved bell tower on the Adriatic coast. The clock is also unusual, as its face shows 24 hours rather than the usual 12. A small church was built above the gate in the 6th century, and the gate was later used as a courthouse area and a market of small shops. The best view is from Narodni trg (People's Square), where the arch, clock tower and surrounding buildings fit into one frame. The gate sits on a narrow lane and is easy to miss in crowds, so arriving early or late gives you a clearer view. For a quieter, closer picture, look up at the vaulted arch from Ispod ure, or step into the passage and frame the square through the opening.
text.geographic_location: The Iron Gate is on the western side of the old town in Split, in the walls of Diocletian's Palace, facing Narodni trg (People's Square).
text.directions_text: Head for the western edge of Split's old town, the area around Diocletian's Palace, and make for Narodni trg (People's Square). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the gate, clock tower and square buildings together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the close upward view of the arch, and to telephoto (2x or more) for details such as the clock face.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Narodni trg (west side of the square, facing the gate). The gate's arched stone front and the medieval clock tower beside it, framed by the People's Square buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the arch and tower upright, with the tower on one side and the arch near the centre. Keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean. For a quieter alternative, try Ispod ure for a close, upward view of the vaulted arch and the later building pressed against it. You can also step into the gate's passage and frame the square through the opening.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out. Use the ultra-wide only up close, as it can stretch the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Arrive early or late in the day, when the narrow lane is less crowded and the gate is easier to see clearly.

text.access_note: The gate and square are in the public old town.
claims_not_in_sources: The gate's passage and Narodni trg are public walkways in the old town that can be entered without a ticket.
The ultra-wide lens can stretch objects near the edges of the frame.
Dragging the exposure slider down can stop a bright sky washing out.
